title: उत्तराखण्ड में बारिश, ओलावृष्टि और तेज हवाओं की संभावना - liveskgnews

full_text:
देहरादून : उत्तराखण्ड में मौसम को लेकर ताजा अपडेट सामने आया है। पौड़ी गढ़वाल समेत देहरादून, हरिद्वार, टिहरी और उत्तरकाशी के कुछ इलाकों में गरज-चमक के साथ बिजली गिरने, ओलावृष्टि और तेज हवाएं चलने की संभावना जताई गई है। मौसम संबंधी अलर्ट के अनुसार, हवा की रफ्तार 40 से 50 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटा तक पहुंच सकती है।
पौड़ी गढ़वाल में आज कैसा रहेगा मौसम?
आज पौड़ी गढ़वाल में दिन के समय धुंधली धूप रहने का अनुमान है। तापमान लगभग 12 से 24 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रह सकता है। हालांकि, मौसम विभाग की चेतावनी के मद्देनजर स्थानीय मौसम में बदलाव की संभावना को नजरअंदाज नहीं किया जा सकता।
इन जिलों में भी मौसम को लेकर सतर्कता
मौसम संबंधी चेतावनी में देहरादून, हरिद्वार, पौड़ी गढ़वाल, टिहरी गढ़वाल और उत्तरकाशी के कुछ स्थानों पर गरज-चमक, आकाशीय बिजली, ओलावृष्टि और तेज झोंकेदार हवाओं की आशंका जताई गई है।
ऐसे मौसम में खुले स्थानों पर रहने, पेड़ों के नीचे खड़े होने और बिजली चमकने के दौरान असुरक्षित स्थानों पर रुकने से बचना चाहिए।
मौसम विभाग की चेतावनी के बीच लोगों से सावधानी बरतने की अपील
पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में मौसम तेजी से बदल सकता है। ऐसे में वाहन चालकों और पहाड़ी मार्गों पर यात्रा करने वाले लोगों को विशेष सावधानी बरतने की सलाह दी जाती है। यात्रा से पहले सड़क की स्थिति और मौसम संबंधी आधिकारिक अपडेट जरूर जांचें।

full_text:
Cider producers say increasingly hot summers are shrinking harvests and making apple crops harder to predict, as many brace themselves for the worst year on record.
Growers described they have been taking to their orchards unprecedently early over the last few years, as apples are dropping weeks before they are expected to be ready.
The time to pick apples depends very much on their variety, but many are typically ready by October, in line with peak harvest season.
Paul Harrison, producer of Temple Cider, near Beaminster, described as a result of the hot summer and drought, they have reaped smaller quantities of apples, that are falling nearly a month earlier than anticipated.
“Everything we do is handpicked and pressed in small batches, he said, “this summer the early apples are coming earlier than usual. About two to three weeks earlier.
“Last year was early and this year was earlier again.”
As well as making smaller fruit, the apples that do make it to pressing contain higher sugar levels, leading to a stronger cider, which for some suppliers is of no use as pubs will not sell it.
The hot weather has also affected pears that they grow for perry, which are ready and dropping a month earlier as well.
This summer was provisionally the hottest the UK has ever experienced, according to the Met Office, which was not only sweltering but long lasting, with six heatwaves from May to August.
Throughout the summer, some apple growers across the UK resulted in smearing produce with clay, to act as a type of sun protection, to prevent them from boiling from the inside out.
As an independent, smaller business, Paul said they were lucky to be able to adapt their practices and use any of the 35 varieties of apples that thrived over others when needed, but initially, they did have their worries.
He said that larger companies are not always quite so lucky, and in the past, some had reached out to see if they would sell any of their harvest.
Paul said: “I have been told stories of orchards that should be yielding 50 tonnes of apples and have got half of that.”
Not only are harsh summers a threat for cider makers, but milder winters also mean that some flowers cannot bud in the spring which will stunt fruition later in the year, particularly for the Dabinett variety.
“Most apples need a certain number of chilled hours in the winter, below 5 or 6 degrees. They will be adversely affected by milder winters,” Paul said.
Dorset was officially declared in drought this summer in what was described as an ‘exceptionally serious situation’ following the driest July on record since they began in 1836.
Paul, who was out picking apples while taking to the News, said will be collecting the last apples towards the last week of October.
He runs Temple Cider alongside his partner Jo Taylor. The couple moved to the farm in 2014 and incorporated cider making into their business. Paul was previously an electrical engineer and is originally from Derbyshire.
All the apples used are picked by hand and the business has won a number of impressive awards, including a gold medal from the International Cider Challenge last year.
“This is my favourite time, spending time in the orchard picking up apples. I look forward to it every year. Everybody thinks I am crazy, picking everything up by hand. We are not working on an industrial scale. It’s a life crawling around on your hands and knees,” Paul said.

full_text:
On Monday evening, a surge of excitement rippled through niche online communities where self-proclaimed home battery enthusiasts congregate. Users flocked to Reddit to share triumphs and screenshots reflecting substantial profits accrued that afternoon from trading on the National Energy Market (NEM). Electricity prices in New South Wales (NSW) experienced an abrupt spike around 3:30 PM AEDT, reaching an astonishing peak of $23,107 per megawatt hour (MWh), just shy of the market cap. This surge saw prices exceed $5,000/MWh during 11 distinct five-minute intervals.
A typical Australian household consumes between 15 to 20 kilowatt hours of electricity daily. As temperatures soared into the mid-30s Celsius, reaching a staggering 34.7 degrees at Observatory Hill in Sydney—over 12 degrees above the long-term monthly average—homes equipped with solar panels and batteries seized the opportunity to sell power back to the grid at higher rates.
Tristan Edis, CEO of Green Energy Markets, interpreted the price escalation as indicative of a vulnerability within the NEM, particularly amid climatic shifts and aging coal plants. “It’s normal for electricity prices to be high when temperatures exceed 30 degrees,” Edis explained, adding that such spikes in October are unexpected.
Various factors contributed to this extraordinary price surge. With rising temperatures, several coal-fired generation units were either offline or operating at reduced capacity. Specifically, four out of NSW’s 12 coal units were out of commission, and high transmission lines were unable to operate at full capacity due to maintenance work. This situation hindered the delivery of renewable energy precisely when it was needed most, causing an excess of renewable energy and storage capacity to be curtailed. Notably, technical curtailment peaked at 2,800 megawatts, significantly impacting renewable and battery sources in Southern NSW.
During this period of heightened demand, prices fluctuated unpredictably. Following an initial rise from about $200/MWh to over $1,300/MWh and then to the $23,000 threshold, the market experienced erratic price oscillations, reflective of the intensified demand against diminished supply.
Dave Smith, a wholesale power market designer, noted that household batteries increasingly became a crucial component of the energy landscape. The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) sets prices based on bids from electricity generators every five minutes, but the burgeoning fleet of household batteries operates “behind the meter,” making them invisible to AEMO’s oversight. When prices surged, home battery owners swiftly sold power back to the grid, creating an unpredictable but potentially lucrative market response.
Co-CEO of Amber Electric, Dan Adams, reported that revenue generated by battery owners that day might well have set a record, with approximately $2 million earned within just two hours. Each of the 30,000 participating customers averaged about $69, while top earners pocketed over $500.
Looking to the future, analysts pointed out that the ongoing integration of large and small battery technologies is reshaping energy production, consumption, and pricing. AEMO’s recent energy plan highlighted that home battery installations have surged to about 600,000, with projections suggesting over two million by 2030. Though the average wholesale price has significantly decreased recently, the irregular price behavior exhibited on Monday underscores the necessity for improved coordination and visibility of home batteries within the grid.
The Australian energy landscape is bracing for a potentially record hotter summer, influenced by an El Niño weather pattern, further complicating the reliance on aging coal generators. As discussions surrounding energy sustainability escalate, the importance of building out transmission infrastructure alongside expanding battery storage capacity becomes increasingly clear. Analysts emphasize that while household batteries have much to offer, their full potential can only be realized through a comprehensive approach that addresses energy generation and management challenges.
